b: Bill Watterson is one of the most outstanding cartoonists of our times, and his work is being celebrated at a big exhibit that just opened at the Norman Rockwell Museum. It’s called “Exploring Calvin and Hobbes” and it features over 133 original works by Watterson.

The artwork itself is beautifully presented. You can see from the originals that Bill Watterson works neatly, without much white-out, about two times up. Many of the classic characters are in evidence, not only Calvin and and his tiger-friend Hobbes, but also Miss Wormwood, Moe, and Calvin’s parents.
There are some of the classic Sunday pages and some memorable scenarios, like the Transmogrifier box and the amazing dinosaur art from around 1993.

The show includes some of Watterson’s heroes and influences, such as Walt Kelly’s Pogo, Charles Schultz’s Peanuts, Alex Raymond’s Flash Gordon, and there’s a whole room full of Krazy Kat by George Herriman.

One display case contains a few art supplies that Bill Watterson uses, such as dip pens, brushes, and ink. There are a couple tiny plein air sketches from 1995, and there is a handout inviting kids to create their own characters.

But that’s about it. It’s a pretty basic, stripped-down exhibition, just the art in simple black frames. There’s not much insight into his creative process, his battles with corporate interests, or his personal reflections.
I wasn’t expecting to see a photo of Bill Watterson, because we all know he’s camera-shy and media-averse. And I wasn’t expecting Mr. Watterson to do any events or lectures at the museum.

The exhibit could have done so much more without showing his face or betraying his privacy. I would have liked to see a video of his hand drawing his characters. Or a photo of his studio with an empty chair. Or a few 4-foot-tall blowups of Hobbes dancing. Or some examples of work that didn’t get published. Or some sketches or roughs or preliminaries that reveal his process. Or an explanation of why he quit the comic after ten years, and what he’s been doing since. Or a guest book. Or a cartoon wall to let his fans thank him.
I drew these versions of Calvin with a face (and without one) for my 5-year-old granddaughter to complete.
To download this as an 8.5x11 inch image you can share with a kid in your life, here’s a link to Google Drive.

I respect Bill Watterson’s desire to not license or commercialize his characters. Animators have always drooled over his dynamic poses, and action scenarios. But it would have been nice to hear him at least express his frustration with the commercialization of animation characters. What was missing for me was the fun that the strip embodies. And since the strip was retired more than 30 years ago, there’s a risk that a new generation will have forgotten the strip. Let’s hope this show brings back an interest in his comics.

Some aspects of this gap are addressed by a 35-page interview in the catalog from 2014. The interview is conducted by the show’s curator, Jenny Robb of the Billy Ireland Cartoon Library and Museum in Ohio.

Watterson’s thoughts appear in a Comics Journal interview and an earlier publication called The 10th Anniversary Book. That book gets into more detail about his frustrations with the formatting issues that syndicates forced him to abide by. He says that modern syndication requirements dictated “specific and unyielding” panel dimensions so editors could easily crop or rearrange strips to fit shrinking page real estate, forcing cartoonists to dedicate the top row to an expendable “throwaway” gag.
Because of those fixed panel borders, Watterson noted that he would:
“...often need to eliminate dialogue or simplify the drawings so they’d fit in the arbitrary space the format allotted.”
After he took a sabbatical, the newspapers relented, and gave him more freedom, and his exuberance in later Sunday panels is palpable.
I recommend the show if you love the characters and don’t mind spending $25 for adult entrance fee. Discounts are available.
I was just hoping for a little more meat in the sandwich, so I came away a little hungry.

The exhibition “Exploring Calvin & Hobbes” will be on view at the Norman Rockwell Museum through May 31, 2027, after which it’ll go to the Brandywine River Museum in Pennsylvania in late 2027. They’re looking to extend it after that, so if you’re involved with a museum elsewhere, contact the Billy Ireland Cartoon Art Library Museum.
